title: Closing Day: Documents, Wire Fraud Prevention & Possession

slides.title: Check every figure, verify every wire by voice, and collect every key before you leave
slides.subtitle: Lesson PA.11. Closing Day: Documents, Wire Fraud Prevention & Possession
meta: Education only. Not legal, lending, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
This is closing day. It's the day you move the most money you'll move in this whole program, so we're going to slow it down.

After this lesson you can check your final closing figures line by line against your accepted offer and your latest loan terms. You'll know which document does what. You'll know how to send your closing funds without handing them to a scammer. And you'll know what to collect when the keys to your short-term rental change hands.

You'll leave with three tools: a closing-figures comparison, a closing-day checklist, and an unresolved items log that carries into PA.12.

Cedar Ridge is our example again. Every line-item fee I show you is an assumption, built to add up to the example's totals. None of this is legal, lending, or insurance advice.

slides.title: Money, documents, and control change hands at closing, and they have to move in order

nodes.d: To the seller, the seller's lender, the title company, and service providers.
The deed moves ownership to you. The lender gets a claim on the house.
Accounts, records, and the right to occupy.

box.label: This fails if
box.text: You wire before you check the figures, sign before the walkthrough, or get the deed without the lock codes.

slides.notes:
Closing looks like a pile of signatures. Underneath, three things move.

Money moves from you and your lender to the seller, the seller's lender, the title company, and a list of service providers.

Documents move ownership to you and give your lender a claim on the house.

Control moves too. Keys, codes, accounts, records, and the right to occupy.

A title company or a closing attorney runs the closing. I'll call the person handling your file there the settlement agent.

Most closing problems come from one of those three getting ahead of the others. You wire money before you've checked the figures. You sign before the walkthrough. You get the deed but not the lock codes.

This lesson puts them in order: check the figures, walk the house, review the documents, verify the wire by voice, and sign what matches. Then collect control before you leave. Ask your settlement agent early whether your funds must arrive before or after you sign.

slides.title: A DSCR loan may not come with a Closing Disclosure, so ask which document you'll get

left.head: Most consumer mortgages
left.note: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) rules apply.
items: A Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing
Compare it with your Loan Estimate
Don't close until you've received and reviewed it

right.head: Business-purpose credit
right.note: Such as a non-owner-occupied rental on a DSCR (debt service coverage ratio) loan.
items: Such as a DSCR (debt service coverage ratio) loan
Falls outside many consumer disclosure rules
You may get a settlement statement instead
Owner stays over 14 days a year: not treated as a non-owner-occupied rental

box.label: Ask in writing, early
box.text: Which closing document will I receive? When will final figures arrive? Ask the lender and title company for them 3 business days ahead anyway.

slides.notes:
For most consumer mortgages, the lender must give you a Closing Disclosure. That's its final form listing your loan terms and costs. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the CFPB, says you must receive it at least three business days before closing. That window lets you compare it with your Loan Estimate, the lender's early estimate. Don't close until you've received and reviewed it.

Investment property adds a wrinkle. The CFPB's official commentary treats credit to buy a non-owner-occupied rental as business-purpose credit. That falls outside many of the consumer disclosure rules. A debt service coverage ratio, or DSCR, loan is sized mostly on the property's income. It's the usual case here. So its lender may give you a title company settlement statement instead.

A vacation home the owner occupies more than 14 days in the coming year doesn't get that treatment. So give your lender an honest personal-use number. Our example buyers, Maya and Chris, plan about 10 days.

Ask your lender early, in writing: which document will I get, and when? Ask for final figures three business days ahead anyway.

slides.title: Compare the final figures in four groups, plus the names, against what you agreed
rows: Price, earnest money, seller credit, repair escrow, items left
Loan amount, rate, points, P&I, term, prepayment penalty
Each fee by section; title charges; owner's policy
Loan Estimate or written quote; title quote
Insurance premium, prepaid interest, escrow balance

box.label: The CFPB's test
box.text: Cash to close should match your Loan Estimate or written quote. If it doesn't, ask the lender why.

slides.notes:
Work through four groups, then the names.

Our running example is Cedar Ridge, a hypothetical three-bedroom lake house. Maya and Chris are buying it for $385,000 as a short-term rental.

The first group is deal terms from your contract. Price, earnest money credit, any seller credit, any repair escrow, and anything the seller agreed to leave. For Cedar Ridge, the PA.9 amendment has the seller fixing the septic and treating the well before closing. The seller also pays a $3,100 contractor's lien found in the title search. That payoff belongs on the seller's side, not yours.

The second group is loan terms, including principal and interest, or P&I. Compare each one against the written quote you accepted in PA.7. A rate or point change needs an explanation.

The third group is closing costs, fee by fee. If your loan came without a Loan Estimate, use the lender's written quote. Your title charges should match the title company's quote.

The fourth is prepaids and escrow. Check that the insurance premium is the STR policy from PA.9, not a generic homeowners estimate.

Finally, the names must match your PA.10 worksheet exactly.

slides.title: Most of Cedar Ridge's lender and title fees matched the estimate, and four moved
rows: B. Appraisal with STR rent analysis
slides.caption: A = origination, B = services you couldn't shop for, C = services you shopped for, E = government fees. Letters follow Closing Disclosure sections; D is omitted.
slides.notes:
For this example, Maya and Chris closed on their backup DSCR loan. That's an assumption. $385,000 price. $288,750 loan at 7.25% with 1 point, meaning 1% of the loan paid up front. Down payment $96,250. Total closing costs including points, $14,438. Cash to close, $110,688.

The example's assumptions give only the total: 3% of price, plus 1 point. This table is one plausible breakdown. Every line item is an assumption. Real fees vary by state, lender, and title company.

I've laid it out in Closing Disclosure sections so you can see the structure. On a DSCR loan you may not get a Loan Estimate or Closing Disclosure. Then you compare the lender's written fee quote with the title company's settlement statement. The estimate column stands for whichever early estimate you got. A is origination, B and C are services you couldn't and could shop for, and E is government fees. D is left out here.

Four lines moved here. The appraisal, the lender's title policy, the settlement fee, and the survey. I'll explain why each moved in two slides.

slides.title: Closing costs total $14,438, so cash to close is $110,688, $659 over the estimate
slides.caption: F = prepaids, G = initial escrow deposit, H = other. Check: $2,888 points + $11,550 other costs (3% of $385,000) = $14,438. Plus $96,250 down = $110,688.
slides.notes:
Here's the second half. F is prepaids, and G is the initial escrow deposit. H is other costs, including the owner's title policy if you chose it in PA.9.

The final column adds up to the example's totals. Points of $2,888 plus $11,550 of other costs equals $14,438. The $11,550 is 3% of $385,000. Add the $96,250 down payment and you get $110,688.

The prepaid interest line uses the daily rate. $288,750 times 7.25%, divided by 365, is about $57.35 a day. Ten days is about $574. Fifteen days is about $860. That's why it moved.

The escrow lines use $3,850 a year of property tax and $3,200 of insurance. Your lender sets how many months go into the starting balance. If the months look high, ask how it calculated them.

Always do this addition yourself. If your sum doesn't match the statement, that's your first question for the settlement agent.

slides.title: The real STR insurance policy added $700; a later closing date took back $286
slides.side:
Insurance lines: +$700.

Other fees: +$245.

Later closing date: -$286.

$700 + $245 - $286 = $659, the gap between the two totals.

side_box.label: Every change has a reason
side_box.text: Write the reason and who gave it next to each line.

slides.notes:
Now read the changes the way you would at your kitchen table.

Insurance went up $600, and its escrow line up $100. The estimate used a generic homeowners premium of $2,600. The final figures use the actual STR quote of $3,200 from PA.9. That's the right policy. Those two lines add $700, more than the whole net change.

One caution. This $3,200 is the same first-year premium already in the Cedar Ridge operating budget. If you add up year-one cash, include it once, either here or in operating costs, not both.

The appraisal went up $100. Ask the lender whether that increase is allowed under the rules for your loan.

The lender's title policy and settlement fee went up $95 combined, and the survey $50. They shopped for these, so ask the title company and surveyor to explain each one.

Prepaid interest went down $286, because the closing date moved later in the month. That's the one line that went down.

Add it up and you get $659. Every dollar of change has a reason.

slides.title: After the $7,700 earnest money credit, Cedar Ridge's wire is $102,988

lines.label: Earnest money paid at contract (2% of price)

slides.side:
Checks outside the fee table: the seller's septic and well invoices should be in the file. The $3,100 lien payoff should sit on the seller's side. Names should match your PA.10 worksheet.

Your statement may label this figure differently, or its cash-to-close line may already subtract the deposit.

side_box.label: Guard this number
side_box.text: Confirm with the settlement agent, by voice at the saved number, that this is the wire amount on your statement.

slides.notes:
Next, the wire amount. Suppose Maya and Chris paid $7,700 of earnest money at contract. That's 2% of price, and it's an assumption. The deposit is credited at closing.

So the funds they still owe are $110,688 minus $7,700. That's $102,988. That's the number they'll wire, and it's the number a scammer would love to redirect.

Your statement may show this figure under a different label. Its cash-to-close line may already subtract the deposit. So before wiring, confirm with the settlement agent which figure is the wire amount. By voice, at the saved number.

A few checks aren't in the fee table. The seller's septic and well invoices should be in the file. The $3,100 lien payoff should be on the seller's side. The names should match PA.10.

And the monthly payment should read $1,970 principal and interest, about $2,557 with escrow. Tax of $3,850 plus insurance of $3,200, divided by 12, is $587.50 a month.

slides.title: Walk the house against your PA.9 tracker before you sign anything
items: Seller repairs: see the septic work and the new well UV (ultraviolet) system, and get both invoices.
Included items: furniture, appliances, dock equipment, anything else in the contract.
New damage: water stains, broken windows, storm damage that wasn't there at inspection.
Systems: run every tap, flush toilets, test HVAC in both modes, check the water heater.
Photos and meters: photograph each room; write down utility meter readings with the time.

box.label: If you find a real problem
box.text: Don't sign and hope. Call your agent, and your attorney if you have one. Common fixes are a repair escrow, a credit, or a short delay.

slides.notes:
The CFPB says to use the final walkthrough to confirm agreed repairs were made. It also says to check that items the seller agreed to leave are still there. If something's wrong, contact the seller right away.

For an STR, the walkthrough is also your first look at the house as an operator. So bring the PA.9 tracker and walk it row by row.

Look at the seller's repairs, and get the invoices. Check the included items. Look for new damage. Run the systems. Then photograph every room and write down the meter readings with the time. You'll use those for the final bills and in the PA.12 handoff.

If you find a real problem, don't sign and hope. Call your agent, and your attorney if you have one. The CFPB notes you can walk away at closing, but you might lose your deposit and face other consequences under your contract. Let your attorney or agent use that lever. Don't try it alone at the table.

slides.title: Know what each closing document does before you initial a single page
rows: Transfers ownership to the title owner you chose. Gets recorded.
When you'll get the recorded copy
The borrower's promise to repay on its terms
Gives the lender a claim on the house
Due-on-sale clause: lender can demand full payment if title moves without consent (PA.10)
Your personal promise to repay if your LLC doesn't, on a loan made to the LLC
Read it with your attorney before closing day
Shows every dollar in and out
Initial only after it matches your comparison
Not signed, but the lender needs it
Effective on or before closing; names match
slides.notes:
You'll sign a stack. Know what the main pieces do, and read the names on each one against your PA.10 worksheet.

The deed transfers ownership to the title owner you chose. It gets recorded with the county. Ask the title company when you'll get the recorded copy.

The promissory note is the promise to repay. Read the rate, payment, maturity, and any prepayment section.

The mortgage or deed of trust gives the lender a claim on the house. It holds the due-on-sale clause from PA.10, which lets the lender demand full payment if the property moves without its consent.

An entity loan is made to your LLC, not to you. If the lender wants a personal guaranty, you promise to repay if the LLC doesn't. Read it with your attorney before closing day.

Initial the settlement statement only after it matches your comparison. And check that the insurance binder starts on or before closing, with the right names.

slides.title: Set up trusted contacts at contract, then verify every wire by voice at a saved number

nodes.d: Such as your agent and settlement agent. Save numbers from a card in hand or a site you typed.
Ask for it on every call about money. No phrase? Hang up and call the saved number.
Call the saved number. Read back bank, account name, number, and amount.
Call the saved number again. Confirm the exact amount.

box.label: Cedar Ridge
box.text: Maya and Chris saved the settlement agent's number from the title company's website at contract and agreed on a code phrase. Their bank's wire form gets filled in only after the voice readback.

slides.notes:
Closing-day wire fraud targets exactly your situation. A known closing date, a large transfer, and several parties emailing each other. The CFPB warns that scammers send emails posing as your agent or settlement agent with last-minute changes to wiring instructions.

Here's how I'd turn the CFPB's guidance into a protocol.

Set it up early. At contract, identify two trusted people who can confirm payment instructions. Your agent and your settlement agent are the natural pair. Write down their numbers from a source you trust: a card handed to you, or a company website you typed in yourself.

Agree on a code phrase only they know. Ask for it on every call about money. If the caller can't give it, hang up and call the saved number.

Before you send anything, call the settlement agent at the saved number and read back the bank name, account name, account number, and amount.

After the wire, call the saved number again and confirm they received the exact amount.

slides.eyebrow: Wire fraud · red flags and response
slides.title: Treat any change to wiring instructions as fraud until a saved number proves otherwise
items: A 'new account' email is the classic move. Stop and call the saved number.
Don't email financial information. The CFPB says email is never a secure way to send it.
Don't trust caller ID. Scammers can spoof numbers. Hang up and call the saved number.
If a wire goes wrong, act in minutes. Call your bank or wire service right away to try to stop or reverse it.
File a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3).
slides.notes:
The rest of the protocol is about what to do when something feels off.

Treat any change as fraud until proven otherwise. A 'new account' email is the classic move. Don't reply to it. Stop and call the saved number.

Don't email financial information. The CFPB says email is never a secure way to send it.

Don't trust caller ID. The CFPB notes scammers can spoof phone numbers. If a call feels wrong, hang up and call the saved number yourself.

And if something does go wrong, minutes matter. The CFPB says to contact your bank or wire service immediately to try to stop or reverse the transfer. It also says to file a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center.

For Cedar Ridge, the wire is $102,988. Ask your bank this week who to call, and what their cutoff times are, so you aren't looking it up in a panic.

slides.title: Collect six things before you leave the closing or the house
items: Physical keys, garage remotes, mailbox keys, gate or boat-launch passes
Door and alarm codes; admin logins for smart devices. You reset every code.
Warranties and manuals: roof, HVAC, water heater, appliances, septic parts, well UV system
Vendor records: septic and well invoices, water tests, pest, HVAC, plow, trash
Permits: STR permit status for your new application, septic permit record, past building permits
Proof of payment: final figures, wire confirmation, title documents, insurance declarations

box.label: Anything missing
box.text: Goes on the unresolved items log, with an owner and a date. That log is the bridge to PA.12.

slides.notes:
The deed gets recorded in the county records after closing. Control transfers only when you have every way into the house and every record about it. Your contract says when possession passes.

Collect six things before you leave the closing or the house that day.

Physical keys and passes. Codes and admin logins for every smart device. Ask the seller to remove their accounts from each device, and then reset every code yourself.

Warranties and manuals, including the well UV system the seller installed. Vendor records, like the septic invoices, water tests, and the names of the seller's plow and trash services. Permit records.

And proof of payment: the final figures, the wire confirmation, your title documents, and the insurance declarations. Ask the title company when you'll receive the final owner's and lender's title policies.

Anything you don't get goes on the unresolved items log. Every row needs an owner and a date.

slides.title: Fill in the closing-figures comparison before you send a single dollar
slides.caption: Selected rows. The full 18-line table is in the written lesson. Write n/a where a column doesn't apply.
slides.notes:
The exercise has three parts. This is part A, the closing-figures comparison.

The full table in the lesson has 18 lines. I've pulled the ones that matter most onto the slide. For each line, fill in what the accepted offer or PA.9 amendment says. Then add what your latest loan quote says, and what the final figures say. Then mark whether they match.

The first row is a model. Cedar Ridge's price is $385,000 in the offer and in the final figures. The loan quote doesn't state a price, so that cell says n/a. Write n/a wherever a column doesn't apply.

Not under contract yet? Practice with the Cedar Ridge figures from the worked example.

The full version also has a column for the question you asked, the answer, and the date. Don't send the wire until every row either matches or has a written answer.
slides.text: Write n/a where a column doesn't apply. Not under contract yet? Practice with the Cedar Ridge figures.

slides.title: Tick eleven steps from contract to keys, with a date and time for each
items: **Contract:** contacts and code phrase set up
**Contract:** asked which document, and when
**3+ days before:** final figures received
**3+ days before:** table A done
**3+ days before:** binder and names checked
**Closing day:** walkthrough and photos
**Closing day:** read deed, note, mortgage, guaranty
**Closing day:** wire instructions verified by voice
**Closing day:** wire sent; receipt confirmed by voice
**Handover:** keys, codes, remotes, records, permits
**Handover:** codes reset; seller accounts removed
slides.notes:
Part B is the closing-day checklist. Eleven steps, in the order they happen, from contract to keys.

Two happen at contract. Set up your trusted contacts and code phrase. And ask the lender which closing document you'll get and when the final figures arrive.

Three happen at least three business days before closing. Receive the final figures, finish table A, and confirm the insurance binder's date and names.

Four happen on closing day, before you sign. Walk the house. Review the deed, note, mortgage, and any guaranty. Verify the wire instructions by voice. Then send the wire and confirm receipt by voice.

The last two happen at handover. Collect control, and reset every code.

Ask your settlement agent whether your funds must arrive before or after you sign. Fill in the date and time for each step as you go.

slides.title: Start the unresolved items log at closing, because it carries straight into PA.12
slides.text: Cedar Ridge starts with three rows (example rows are assumptions). Give each row one owner and one due date.
rows: Arrives after the county records the deed
Seller's permit doesn't transfer; new owner applies
Needs a clean result before the first guest

box.label: The rule
box.text: Every row gets one owner and one due date. The log goes with you into PA.12's handoff packet.

slides.notes:
Part C is the unresolved items log. This is the bridge to PA.12.

For Cedar Ridge, three rows start the log. The recorded deed copy, which arrives after the county records the deed. The new STR permit application, because the seller's permit didn't transfer. And the well retest after treatment, because the seller's UV system needs a clean result before the first guest. All three are assumptions for teaching.

Your log will have its own rows. Anything you didn't collect at possession goes here. Anything the walkthrough turned up that's being fixed after closing goes here.

Every row gets one owner and one due date. Not 'we.' One name. Then take this log, and the PA.9 tracker, into the next lesson.

slides.title: Five parties confirm the figures, the wire, the documents, and the coverage
rows: Which closing document you'll get and when, why any rate, point, or fee changed, the loan figures behind the wire amount
Settlement figures, lien payoffs, recording, title policies, the exact wire amount and instructions, verified by voice at a saved number
Possession terms, walkthrough remedies, anything in the documents that differs from your contract
Policy effective date, named insured, mortgagee clause
Its wire process, cutoff times, and who to call immediately if a wire must be stopped
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what on closing day.

Your lender confirms which closing document you'll get and when. It explains any change to the rate, points, or fees. It confirms the loan figures behind the wire amount.

The title company or closing attorney confirms the settlement figures, the lien payoffs, recording, and the title policies. It also confirms the exact wire amount and the wire instructions. Always by voice, at the number you saved.

Your attorney or agent confirms possession terms and what you can do if the walkthrough turns something up. They also flag anything in the documents that differs from your contract.

Your insurer confirms the effective date, the named insured, and the mortgagee clause.

And your bank confirms how its wires work, its cutoff times, and who you call right away if a wire has to be stopped.

slides.title: Set up your wire protection and your comparison table before closing week
items: Email your lender: which closing document, and when will final figures arrive?
Save the settlement agent's number from a trusted source; agree on a code phrase.
Call your bank and write down its wire cutoff time and its fraud line.
Copy table A and fill in the offer, amendment, and loan-quote columns now.
slides.next: Next: PA.12 Your Post-Close Checklist. Bring your unresolved items log and the PA.9 tracker.
slides.notes:
Four things this week. None of these takes long.

First, email your lender and ask which closing document you'll get and when the final figures will arrive.

Second, save the settlement agent's number from a source you trust, and agree on a code phrase.

Third, call your bank. Write down its wire cutoff time and the number to call if a wire needs to be stopped.

Fourth, copy table A and fill in the first two columns now, from your offer, your PA.9 amendment, and your loan quote. When the final figures arrive, you only have one column left.

After closing, you own the house. It isn't a rental yet. PA.12 Your Post-Close Checklist covers the insurance, utilities, safety work, and a dated handoff packet. Bring your unresolved items log and the PA.9 tracker. Most of what's still open lands there.

slides.notes:
The closing-disclosure, walkthrough, and wire-fraud guidance comes from the CFPB pages on this slide. That includes the three-business-day Closing Disclosure rule, the business-purpose treatment of rental loans, and the wire fraud steps.

The document descriptions and the possession list are practical checklists. Confirm them with your title company and your attorney.

Each page was checked on September 25, 2026. Confirm the wording on the before, during, and after closing page yourself before you quote it.

The Cedar Ridge financing figures come from our running example. The line-item breakdown, the estimate figures, and the earnest money are assumptions, built to add up to the example's totals. Your closing will have different fees, a different order, and possibly a different document. The comparison method stays the same.
